10. Comparability Over Time and Space

Observed data have been collected and analyzed using consistent methods over space. The satellites that collect the data cover all of North America in their orbital paths. While mapping methods have improved over time, GSL has taken steps to reanalyze older maps to ensure consistency with the latest approach. GSL provides more information about these correction steps. This feature excludes pre-1981 data that were not collected or analyzed with the same methods; hence, it starts with historical observations in 1981.

GCMs inherently use consistent algorithms over time and space.

The observed and projected time series cover the same spatial extent: North America, excluding Greenland. However, they are fundamentally based on different pixel sizes for analysis, as the observed data set uses 24-kilometer pixels while the model resolutions range from less than 1 degree to 2.8 degrees (more than 300 kilometers per side at the equator). As a result of this difference, the project team computed the modeled version of the indicator differently from the observed analysis, as described in Sections 6 and 7 above. This difference was necessary because the observed analysis applies a “50 percent of pixel area” threshold that would not have been practical to apply at the scale of the GCM grid cells.

11. Data Limitations

The technical documentation for the Snow Cover indicator identifies some factors that may impact the confidence, application, or conclusions that readers can draw from the observed portion of this pairing. For example, it notes some of the challenges inherent in detecting snow cover in obscured conditions (thick forest, cloud cover) and small discontinuous patches, which especially reduce confidence in summer measurements.

Future projections of any variable have inherent uncertainty, as described in Section 12 below. Snow cover is influenced by multiple systems and processes, so it may be less direct to model than, say, surface air temperature.

12. Sources of Uncertainty

Observations inevitably reflect measurement uncertainty. Uncertainty measurements are not readily available for this indicator or for the underlying data, but extensive quality assurance/quality control and third-party verification measures show that steps have been taken to minimize uncertainty and ensure that users are able to draw accurate conclusions from the data. Maps based on satellite imagery are often superior to maps based on ground observations, which can be biased due to sparse station coverage—both geographically and in terms of elevation (e.g., a station in a valley will not necessarily have snow cover when nearby mountains do)—and due to the effects of urban heat islands in locations such as airports. Hence, satellite-based maps are generally more representative of regional snow extent, particularly for mountainous or sparsely populated regions.

Model outputs inevitably reflect model uncertainty. Each GCM represents aspects of, and processes within, the climate system differently. These differences will lead to differences in how the GCMs represent both present-day climate and how the climate responds to changes in greenhouse gases. For example, GCMs differ in climate sensitivity, defined as the increase in global temperature when carbon dioxide in the atmosphere doubles relative to pre-industrial times. Even a single GCM will yield different results if presented with different initial conditions, as the chaotic processes within the model will lead to different timing of various modes of variability within the model (such as the El Niño cycle). The shaded bands in the graph for this pairing illustrate this type of uncertainty in the spread of models, as well as year-to-year variations due to internal variability within each model.

Interpreting projections also requires users to consider scenario uncertainty. Projecting future conditions requires assumptions about future greenhouse gas emissions. This feature presents four widely used scenarios to illustrate a range of possibilities without assigning likelihoods to them, nor do these scenarios necessarily bound possible futures.

13. Sources of Variability

Variability in snow cover naturally results from variation in weather patterns, multi-year climate cycles such as the El Niño–Southern Oscillation and Pacific Decadal Oscillation, and other factors. Underlying weekly measurements have even more variability. The construction of this pairing addresses variability in a few ways:

  • Presenting a long-term record (several decades) and calculating annual and seasonal averages to reduce some of the day-to-day “noise” inherent in snow cover measurements.
  • Smoothing GCM outputs with an 11-year moving average.
